endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: UC San Diego Health is leveraging Epic ML tools to predict the likelihood of hospital and patient denial recovery to prioritize human effort on high-value denials and allow automation of low-value denials.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Steps should be taken to ensure that these systems do not override clinical judgment.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Automated PA commonly uses rules-based decision-making in the first level. Rules process simple requests such as a patient’s payer plan and eligibility for treatment.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots in Medicine: A Supplement, Not a Substitute
endorsements.quote: The integration of AI chatbots and medical professionals is more likely to evolve into a collaborative approach, where professionals focus on complex medical decision-making and empathetic patient care while chatbots supplement these efforts.

endorsements.title: Using artificial intelligence to improve administrative process in Medicaid
endorsements.quote: Given these limitations, for now, AI technologies should be used to augment human capabilities until they have proven to be more stable and can be built upon more robust datasets.

endorsements.title: The Infectious Diseases Orchestrator: Embracing AI Literacy in the Agentic Era
endorsements.quote: Simple, well-defined tasks—such as flagging inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions or detecting missing infection control documentations—may be safely handled by AI as first use cases.

endorsements.title: Designing and evaluating large language model-enabled clinical decision support for heart failure: a modular and risk-tiered framework
endorsements.quote: Low-risk tasks such as flagging a missing follow-up appointment or creating patient education from an approved template can be automated with audit logs and clinician override.

evidence.title: Blueprint for Safety: Implementing a Clinically Governed AI Digital Assistant for Patient Guidance
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.outcome: Clinical safety and human routing of inquiries
evidence.effect: Maintained 96% accurate guidance, 0% critical safety events, and reduced human-routed standard-risk queries by 65%.
evidence.quote: Using a randomized rollout to half of the patient population, the authors found that the risk-stratified assistant maintained a high level of clinical safety (96% accurate guidance, 0% critical safety events, and no AI-generated diagnoses) while reducing standard-risk queries routed to human support by 65%, shortening average human response times from 9.6 to 3.6 minutes, and improving resolution of health inquiries without additional visits.

evidence.title: From Concept to Clinic: Real World Evidence for Autonomous AI Deployment in Primary Care Telemedicine
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic concordance restricted to common, lower-complexity conditions
evidence.effect: Concordance was 97.9% in common, lower-complexity conditions meeting the confidence threshold vs 91.3% overall.
evidence.quote: The AI’s top-1 diagnosis matched the clinician’s diagnosis in 91.3% of cases overall, increasing to 96.3% among cases meeting a pre-specified safety confidence threshold, and 97.9% in common, lower-complexity conditions that met the same confidence threshold.

evidence.title: Generative and Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Medical Coding and Billing: A Human-in-the-Loop Architecture and Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Coding accuracy, turnaround time and audit readiness of human-in-the-loop versus manual or fully automated pipelines
evidence.effect: Reported measurable improvements in coding precision, turnaround time, and audit readiness versus manual or fully automated pipelines; no numbers given. Residual hallucination, edge-case misclassification and overreliance risks remained.
evidence.quote: Overall, the findings demonstrate that human-AI collaboration offers a more reliable and accountable pathway than full automation for high-stakes healthcare administration tasks.

evidence.title: Selective prediction as a triage gate for primary-care depression screening: quantifying and mitigating selection bias in CHARLS-2011
evidence.outcome: Selective prediction performance and abstention rate
evidence.effect: All five models: selective prediction at approximately 20% coverage; test AUC 0.90, 95% CI 0.85-0.95; abstained on approximately 80%.
evidence.quote: Model-embedded uncertainty succeeded only for XGBoost; with the decoupled XGBoost residual selector, all five models achieved selective prediction at approximately 20% coverage (test AUC 0.90, 95% CI 0.85-0.95), abstaining on approximately 80% of cases for individual safety.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.effect: AI band-pass: sensitivity 81.7% vs 79.8%, specificity 96.6% vs 96.0%; 779 fewer false positives, 25 more cancers, −80.7% human reads.
evidence.quote: The AI band-pass screening scenario also achieved both higher system sensitivity (81.7%, P < 0.0058) and specificity (96.6%, P < 2.2 × 10 −25 ) than the current standard of care system (Fig. 3 A and Supplementary Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Human-AI collectives most accurately diagnose clinical vignettes
evidence.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic performance after adding physicians
evidence.effect: Adding a single physician increased performance for all LLMs; performance increased steadily with more humans.
evidence.quote: Adding a single physician increased performance for all LLMs even though individual physicians, on average, performed worse than most LLMs; and LLM performance increased steadily with adding more humans.
evidence.sample_unit: text-based medical case vignettes (40,762 physician differential diagnoses)

evidence.title: Deep learning based semi-automated model can predict lineage in patients with pituitary neuroendocrine tumors
evidence.outcome: Lineage accuracy: fully automated vs routing low-confidence cases to IHC/pathologist review
evidence.effect: Fully automated model had a 16.1% accuracy decrease in the prospective cohort (p<0.001). Semi-automated routing gave 95.9% accuracy, comparable to full manual review (p=0.610), with 68.9% workload reduction.
evidence.quote: This significant decrease in manual labor was accompanied by 95.9% in overall accuracy (Fig. 3 ), which was statistically comparable ( p = 0.610) to that achieved through fully IHC staining and manual evaluation by pathologists.

evidence.title: Patient Triage and Guidance in Emergency Departments Using Large Language Models: Multimetric Study
evidence.outcome: Overreliance on patient medical history in department guidance errors
evidence.effect: Physicians attributed 43.42% of overall guidance errors to overreliance on patient medical history rather than current symptoms.
evidence.quote: Another key finding in this part of the experiment was that the guidance provided by ChatGPT (GPT-4o model) was sometimes influenced by the medical history of patients, where physicians attributed 43.42% of the overall guidance error to an overreliance on the medical history of patients.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated patient scenarios (MEWS triage); 264 scenarios for department guidance

evidence.title: Training ChatGPT for surgical decisions: Bariatric surgery analysis using algorithms and evidence
evidence.effect: concordance with clinical practice was 20.0% (Kappa = 0.003; p = 0.96) initially and 25.8% (Kappa = 0.068; p = 0.29) after training
evidence.quote: While potentially useful as an educational tool, ChatGPT is not yet reliable for autonomous surgical decision-making.

evidence.title: Ethical implications of using general-purpose LLMs in clinical settings: a comparative analysis of prompt engineering strategies and their impact on patient safety
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.effect: Level 5: 23.1% critical safety incidents vs Level 1: 2.3%; χ² = 15.7, p < 0.001.
evidence.quote: Level 5 ethical scenarios demonstrated 23.1% critical safety incidents, compared to only 2.3% in Level 1 cases (χ² = 15.7, p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (3 models x 6 prompt strategies x 5 scenarios)

evidence.title: Performance evaluation of 9 large language models in anticoagulation decision-making for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
evidence.venue: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis
evidence.effect: No single model was optimal; HAS-BLED accuracy 8%-51%, regimen selection 33%-89%, monitoring mean 2.55-4.98.
evidence.quote: At present, LLMs may serve as valuable adjuncts to clinical practice but remain unsuitable for use as stand-alone decision-makers.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (100 virtual NVAF patient cases x 9 LLMs)

evidence.title: Concordance between GPT-4 and a multidisciplinary tumor board in pancreatic cancer: A prospective pilot study
evidence.effect: Inadequate capture of clinical complexity by GPT-4 explained three of 12 non-concordant cases (25.0%).
evidence.quote: Among the 12 non-concordant cases, the presumed cause of discordance was an inadequate capture of clinical complexity by GPT-4 in three cases (25.0%), incomplete data in the MDT referral in three cases (25.0%) and a disregard of essential clinical data by GPT-4 in one case (8.3%).

commentary.bottom_line: One randomized trial and one prospective study in real deployments, along with five offline studies, suggest that automating lower-risk or high-confidence cases and routing the rest to humans may preserve accuracy while reducing human workload. The certainty of this evidence is low because tasks and outcomes vary widely, most tests were simulated, and the trial did not report its setting or population.

perspectives.view: One real-deployment randomized trial reported 96% accurate guidance, 0% of the most severe safety events, and 65% fewer standard-risk queries routed to humans, but it did not report setting or population. One prospective study and five offline studies point the same way across unrelated tasks. Consistency favors the practice, while indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to low.

In one pathology cohort, full automation had a 16.1% accuracy decrease prospectively, while routing low-confidence cases to review gave 95.9% accuracy, comparable to full manual review. In hazard studies, the most severe safety incidents rose from 2.3% to 23.1% with case complexity, and autonomous surgical decisions matched practice in 20.0% to 25.8% of cases. These findings support the premise for routing but do not show that it prevents harm.

In one real deployment, concordance was 97.9% for common, lower-complexity conditions that met a confidence threshold, compared with 91.3% across all encounters. One offline study abstained on about 80% of cases to reach an AUC of 0.90. Another reported residual hallucination, edge-case misclassification, and overreliance even with human review in the loop.

Reported workload reductions were 80.7% of human reads in a cancer screening program, 68.9% of pathology review, and 65% of routed standard-risk queries, with screening sensitivity of 81.7% versus 79.8%. Savings depend on how many cases the system defers, and one model deferred about 80%. None of these studies reported costs or staffing requirements.

In a vignette study, adding a single physician improved every language model's diagnostic performance, and performance rose as more humans were added. The trial reduced standard-risk queries routed to humans by 65%, but it did not report who submitted those queries. No study measured patient trust or whether patients who wanted a human reviewer could reach one.

No study testing the practice reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The only hazard study with non-English speakers found that physicians attributed 43.42% of guidance errors to overreliance on medical history. This shows that such problems exist in these groups but does not test routing for them.

commentary.research_gap: No real-deployment trial has compared risk- or confidence-based routing with both full automation and full human review while reporting patient harms, time to human contact, the method used to set routing thresholds, and results by payer, language, and literacy. Studies also have not reported the costs and staffing needed to handle deferred cases.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the seven tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One offline study included older adults in China. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no direct evidence that routing thresholds perform equally well for their patients and would need to monitor performance locally.
